findings.title: Attacker-controlled 32-bit length prefix drives an eager ~2 GiB heap allocation before any data is read (readBytes)
findings.impact: Remote, pre-authentication out-of-memory denial of service against the whole client JVM (not just the AMQP connection), with an amplification factor of roughly 200,000,000:1 between bytes sent and bytes allocated.
findings.evidence: readBytes() reads a 32-bit length from the wire, widens it to unsigned (0..4294967295), and allocates the entire buffer up front: `final long contentLength = unsignedExtend(in.readInt()); if(contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE) { final byte [] buffer = new byte[(int)contentLength]; in.readFully(buffer); ... }`. The declared length is never reconciled with the number of bytes actually available. It is reachable from readLongstr() (field type 'S', line 163) and from the 'x' byte-array field (line 211), both parsed from a TruncatedInputStream inside readTable()/readArray() -- so readFully() will certainly fail, but only AFTER `new byte[]` has already asked the JVM for up to 2,147,483,645 bytes. An 8-byte table entry (0x53 followed by 0x7FFFFFFE) suffices. readTable() is reached from the connection.start server-properties table, i.e. before the client has authenticated the peer, so a malicious or MITM'd broker can trigger it pre-auth; via message headers, any publisher able to set a header on a message the victim consumes can trigger it post-auth across tenants. The negotiated frame-max is no defence: the allocation size depends only on the declared prefix, not on the frame size.
findings.recommendation: Bound the allocation before making it. Check contentLength against a configured ceiling (the client already exposes maxInboundMessageBodySize; a field-level limit belongs here) AND against in.available() / the enclosing TruncatedInputStream's remaining budget, rejecting with MalformedFrameException when the declared length exceeds either. For legitimately large values, read incrementally into a growing buffer capped at the ceiling so heap use tracks bytes actually delivered rather than bytes merely claimed.

findings.title: Unbounded recursion between readFieldValue, readTable and readArray allows StackOverflowError from a single small frame
findings.impact: Remote, pre-authentication denial of service: a StackOverflowError is raised on the connection's frame-reading thread, tearing down the connection (and any Error thrown mid-parse leaves the reader in an undefined state). Cheap and repeatable.
findings.evidence: readFieldValue() dispatches 'F' to readTable() (line 181) and 'A' to readArray() (line 184); both call readFieldValue() again (lines 150 and 245) with no depth counter and no depth limit anywhere in the class. Each nesting level costs only 5 bytes on the wire for an array (type byte 'A' plus a 4-byte length) or 6 bytes for a table, while consuming two-plus JVM stack frames plus a new DataInputStream/TruncatedInputStream pair. With RabbitMQ's default 128 KiB frame-max that is roughly 26,000 achievable levels, well past the ~5,000-10,000 that fit in a default 512 KiB-1 MiB thread stack, so exhaustion is deterministic rather than probabilistic. Same exposure surface as F-001: the connection.start server-properties table (pre-auth) and message header tables (any publisher).
findings.recommendation: Thread an explicit depth parameter through readFieldValue/readTable/readArray and throw MalformedFrameException past a small ceiling (AMQP 0-9-1 field tables in practice nest one or two levels; 8-16 is generous). A depth limit is also the cheapest place to cap the total entry count, which is currently bounded only by the frame size.

findings.title: Declared table/array length is never reconciled with bytes consumed; parsing is driven by available() and can silently drop entries
findings.impact: A malformed frame is accepted as well-formed. A nested table or array that overstates its length can swallow the sibling entries that follow it, so the header map the application sees differs from the bytes on the wire, without any error being raised.
findings.evidence: Both container readers loop on `while(tableIn.available() > 0)` (line 148) and `while(arrayIn.available() > 0)` (line 244) and then return, never asserting that exactly tableLength/length bytes were consumed. TruncatedInputStream caps available() at min(remaining budget, underlying available()), so when the declared length exceeds the bytes actually present the inner loop reads straight through the container boundary into whatever follows, and the enclosing loop then sees available()==0 and returns a silently short map. The class is also public and constructed from an arbitrary DataInputStream (line 57), so if it is ever fed a socket-backed stream rather than a fully-buffered frame payload, available() returning 0 mid-arrival truncates tables with no exception at all. Note that TruncatedInputStream itself is outside the reviewed scope; this analysis relies on its documented min(limit, available) semantics.
findings.recommendation: Track the byte budget explicitly instead of asking available(): loop while consumed < declaredLength, and throw MalformedFrameException if the last field ends past the declared boundary or if the boundary is reached with bytes unconsumed. Also skip any residual bytes so the enclosing stream position stays correct. Do not use available() as a protocol framing signal.

findings.title: Untrusted input path throws an unchecked UnsupportedOperationException instead of MalformedFrameException
findings.impact: A remote peer chooses which exception type the client's I/O thread sees. Callers that correctly handle the declared `throws IOException` contract (and the MalformedFrameException the same method family uses two dozen lines later) will not catch this one, so a protocol-level error escapes as an unexpected runtime failure on the connection thread.
findings.evidence: readBytes() rejects lengths >= Integer.MAX_VALUE with `throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Very long byte vectors and strings not currently supported")`, an unchecked exception raised on fully attacker-controlled input, while the analogous rejection in readFieldValue() (line 217) correctly uses `MalformedFrameException`, which is an IOException. The trigger is a single 4-byte length field of 0x7FFFFFFF or higher.
findings.recommendation: Throw MalformedFrameException (or another IOException) for every rejection driven by wire content, reserving unchecked exceptions for programming errors. Fold this into the size ceiling added for F-001 so one guard covers both cases.

findings.title: Timestamp field is multiplied by 1000 with no overflow check, yielding an attacker-chosen wrapped Date
findings.impact: Silent integer overflow (CWE-190) lets a peer produce a Date whose value bears no relation to the seconds it sent. Applications that use the AMQP timestamp header for freshness, expiry or replay decisions can be made to accept a stale message or reject a fresh one; audit logs record a fabricated time.
findings.evidence: `private static Date readTimestamp(DataInputStream in) throws IOException { return new Date(in.readLong()*1000); }` -- the full 64-bit signed value is read straight off the wire and multiplied, so any |seconds| above ~9.22e15 wraps around silently. The attacker picks the seconds value, hence picks the post-wrap milliseconds value; there is no range validation and no use of Math.multiplyExact.
findings.recommendation: Validate the range before converting (e.g. Math.multiplyExact and translate the ArithmeticException into MalformedFrameException, or reject seconds outside a sane epoch window). Applications making trust decisions on this header should additionally not treat a peer-supplied timestamp as authoritative.

findings.title: Duplicate field-table keys are resolved first-wins and silently discarded
findings.impact: Header desynchronisation. Any intermediary, broker plugin or language runtime in the path that resolves duplicates last-wins will disagree with this client about the value of a repeated header, which is the classic precondition for smuggling a security-relevant header (routing key, tenant id, signature, idempotency key) past a component that inspected the other copy.
findings.evidence: readTable() applies `if(!table.containsKey(name)) table.put(name, value);` -- the first occurrence wins and later occurrences are dropped with no error and no signal to the caller. The AMQP 0-9-1 field-table grammar does not forbid repeated keys on the wire, so the choice is this parser's, and it is not the choice every other AMQP implementation makes.
findings.recommendation: Reject tables containing duplicate keys with MalformedFrameException, which is unambiguous and removes the parser-differential entirely. If backward compatibility forbids that, at minimum document the first-wins rule on the public readTable() API so callers know that a repeated header is invisible to them.

findings.title: Short strings are decoded with the replacement-on-malformed charset overload, so distinct byte sequences collapse to the same String
findings.impact: Invalid UTF-8 in a table key, queue name, exchange name or routing key is accepted and silently rewritten as U+FFFD rather than rejected, so several different wire encodings map to one identical Java String. Downstream code that compares, allowlists or authorises on those strings can be made to match a value the peer never actually sent.
findings.evidence: `private static String readShortstr(DataInputStream in) throws IOException { byte [] b = new byte[in.readUnsignedByte()]; in.readFully(b); return new String(b, "utf-8"); }`. The `String(byte[], String)` constructor is specified to replace malformed and unmappable input rather than throw, and there is no validation of the decoded result. The parser therefore never reports a malformed short string.
findings.recommendation: Decode with an explicit CharsetDecoder configured with CodingErrorAction.REPORT (or StandardCharsets.UTF_8.newDecoder()) and convert a CharacterCodingException into MalformedFrameException. Using StandardCharsets.UTF_8 in place of the "utf-8" string literal is worth doing regardless, as it removes a charset lookup on a hot path.
